title: Book VI: The Widow And The Wife — Chapter LVII
paragraphs:
They numbered scarce eight summers when a name
Rose on their souls and stirred such motions there
As thrill the buds and shape their hidden frame
At penetration of the quickening air:
His name who told of loyal Evan Dhu,
Of quaint Bradwardine, and Vich Ian Vor,
Making the little world their childhood knew
Large with a land of mountain lake and scaur,
And larger yet with wonder, love, belief
Toward Walter Scott who living far away
Sent them this wealth of joy and noble grief.
The book and they must part, but day by day,
In lines that thwart like portly spiders ran
They wrote the tale, from Tully Veolan.

On the evening Fred Vincy walked to Lowick Parsonage, he left at five and called on Mrs. Garth along the way. He wanted to make sure she willingly accepted the new connection between them. He was beginning to realize that even a spirited young man must sometimes walk through this world because he has no horse to carry him.

He found the family, cats and dogs included, beneath the orchard’s great apple tree. For Mrs. Garth it was a festive occasion: her eldest son Christy, her special pride and joy, had come home for a short holiday. Christy thought nothing could be more desirable than becoming a tutor, studying every literature, and turning himself into a new Porson. To poor Fred, he was criticism in human form, an object lesson supplied by that educational mother. Christy himself was a broad-shouldered, square-browed male version of his mother, and barely reached Fred’s shoulder—which made having to acknowledge his superiority still harder. He was completely unpretentious. Fred’s lack of scholarly ambition interested him no more than a giraffe’s would have; he only wished he shared more of Fred’s height. Just now he lay on the ground beside his mother’s chair with his straw hat flat over his eyes. On her other side, Jim was reading aloud from that beloved author responsible for so much happiness in many young lives. The book was “Ivanhoe,” and Jim had reached the great archery scene at the tournament. Ben kept interrupting him. He had fetched his old bow and arrows and, in Letty’s opinion, was making himself horribly disagreeable by demanding that everyone watch his erratic shots. No one wanted to except Brownie, the lively-minded but probably shallow mongrel. The gray-haired Newfoundland lay in the sun and watched with the dull-eyed indifference of extreme old age. Letty’s mouth and pinafore bore slight evidence of her help in gathering the cherries heaped like coral on the tea table. Now she sat wide-eyed on the grass, listening to the story.

Fred Vincy’s arrival changed everyone’s focus. Sitting down on a garden stool, he said he was heading to Lowick Parsonage. Ben dropped his bow, seized an unwilling half-grown kitten instead, stepped over Fred’s outstretched leg, and said, “Take me with you!”
“Me too, please!” Letty said.
“You couldn’t keep up with me and Fred,” said Ben.
“I could. Mother, please tell them I can go,” Letty pleaded. Much of her life consisted of resisting being thought less capable because she was a girl.
“I’m staying with Christy,” Jim remarked, implying that he had got the better of those simpletons. Letty put a hand to her head and looked jealously from one to another, unable to decide.
“Why don’t we all go and see Mary?” Christy said, spreading his arms.

“No, my dear boy, we mustn’t descend on the parsonage in a swarm. And that old Glasgow suit of yours won’t do at all. Besides, your father will be coming home. We must leave Fred to go by himself. He can tell Mary you’re here, and she’ll come back tomorrow.”

Christy looked down at his threadbare knees, then at Fred’s lovely white trousers. Fred’s tailoring certainly made a case for the advantages of an English university. Even looking hot and pushing back his hair with a handkerchief, he managed to be graceful.
“Children, off you go,” said Mrs. Garth. “It’s too warm to crowd round your friends. Take your brother to see the rabbits.”
Her eldest understood and immediately led the children away. Fred realized that Mrs. Garth wanted to let him say whatever he had come to say, but he could only begin with:
“You must be so pleased to have Christy home.”

“Yes, he’s arrived earlier than I expected. He got off the coach at nine, just after his father left. I can’t wait for Caleb to come back and hear how wonderfully Christy is progressing. For the past year he’s covered his expenses by teaching while studying hard himself. He hopes to secure a private tutor’s post soon and travel abroad.”

“He’s a splendid fellow,” Fred said. These cheerful truths tasted like medicine to him. “And never a trouble to anyone.” After a short pause he added, “But I’m afraid you think I’ll be a great deal of trouble to Mr. Garth.”

“Caleb enjoys taking trouble. He’s one of those men who always do more than anyone would have thought to ask,” Mrs. Garth replied. She was knitting, which allowed her to look at Fred or not, just as she pleased—always useful when one wants to load a conversation with improving lessons. Though she meant to be properly restrained, she did want to say something that would do Fred good.

“I know you think I deserve very little, Mrs. Garth, and you’re right,” said Fred, beginning to bristle as he detected a readiness to lecture him. “I’ve managed to behave worst toward the very people I can’t help wanting most from. But while men like Mr. Garth and Mr. Farebrother haven’t given up on me, I don’t see why I should give up on myself.” He thought these male examples might usefully be brought to Mrs. Garth’s attention.
“Certainly,” she said with increasing emphasis. “A young man for whom two such older men had devoted themselves would be seriously at fault if he wasted his life and made their sacrifices useless.”

Her forceful language puzzled Fred a little. He answered only, “I hope that won’t happen to me, Mrs. Garth, now I’ve been given some reason to believe I may win Mary. Mr. Garth told you about that? I don’t suppose it surprised you?” He meant innocently that his own love had probably been plain enough.

“Surprised that Mary had given you encouragement?” Mrs. Garth replied. She thought Fred ought to understand more clearly that, whatever the Vincys might imagine, Mary’s friends could never have wished for this beforehand. “Yes, I admit I was surprised.”
“She never gave me any—not the slightest—when I spoke to her myself,” Fred said, eager to defend Mary. “But when I asked Mr. Farebrother to speak on my behalf, she let him tell me there was hope.”

The impulse to admonish Fred had begun stirring in Mrs. Garth and had not yet found full release. Even _her_ self-control struggled with the sight of this flourishing young man thriving on the disappointments of sadder, wiser people—eating a nightingale without knowing it—while his family imagined hers desperately needed this young sprig. Her irritation had fermented all the more vigorously because she had suppressed it completely with her husband. Exemplary wives sometimes find scapegoats this way. Now she said firmly and forcefully, “Asking Mr. Farebrother to speak for you was a great mistake, Fred.”

“Was it?” Fred instantly went red. He was alarmed but could not understand her meaning. Apologetically he added, “He’s always been such a good friend to us. I knew Mary would listen seriously to him, and he agreed to do it very readily.”

“Yes, young people usually see nothing except their own wishes, and seldom imagine what those wishes cost others,” said Mrs. Garth. She intended to go no further than this beneficial general lesson. Instead, she released her indignation by unnecessarily unwinding her wool and frowning grandly at it.
“I can’t imagine how it could have hurt Mr. Farebrother,” Fred said, though surprising possibilities were already beginning to take shape in his mind.
“Exactly. You can’t imagine,” Mrs. Garth said, clipping each word as neatly as possible.
For a moment Fred stared toward the horizon in anxious dismay. Then he turned abruptly and asked, almost sharply:
“Are you saying Mr. Farebrother’s in love with Mary, Mrs. Garth?”

“If he were, Fred, I should think you’d be the last person to find it surprising,” Mrs. Garth replied. She laid her knitting beside her and folded her arms. Putting her work down was an unusual sign of emotion. Her feelings were, in fact, divided: she was pleased to have taught Fred a lesson, but suspected she had gone too far. He picked up his hat and stick and stood quickly.
“So you think I’m in his way—and Mary’s?” His tone seemed to require an answer.

Mrs. Garth could not reply immediately. She had put herself in the awkward position of being asked to state her real feelings when she knew there were strong reasons to conceal them. The knowledge that she had said too much was particularly humiliating to her. Fred had also displayed an unexpected spark. Now he added, “Mr. Garth seemed glad that Mary cared for me. He can’t have known about this.”
The mention of her husband gave Mrs. Garth a sharp pang. She found the fear of Caleb’s disapproval hard to bear. Hoping to prevent consequences she had never intended, she answered:
“I was only drawing an inference. I have no knowledge that Mary is aware of anything.”

Yet she hesitated to beg him to keep silent about a subject she herself had needlessly introduced. She was unused to humbling herself that way. While she hesitated, another rush of unintended consequences swept beneath the apple tree where the tea things stood. Ben bounded over the grass with Brownie behind him. Seeing the kitten trailing the knitting on a lengthening string of wool, he shouted and clapped. Brownie barked. The desperate kitten leaped onto the tea table, upset the milk, then jumped down and swept half the cherries with it. Ben snatched up the half-knitted sock top and pulled it over the kitten’s head to drive it into a fresh frenzy. Letty arrived, protesting to her mother at the cruelty. It was a chain of events as sensational as “This is the house that Jack built.” Mrs. Garth had to intervene; the other young people joined them, and her private conversation with Fred ended. He escaped as soon as possible. All she could do to suggest some retreat from her severity was say “God bless you” while shaking his hand.

She was painfully aware that she had come close to speaking as “one of the foolish women speaketh”: telling something first, then begging for silence. But she had not begged for silence. To forestall Caleb’s criticism, she decided to criticize herself and confess everything to him that night. It was curious how dreadful a tribunal gentle Caleb could establish for her whenever he chose. Still, she meant to point out that the revelation might do Fred Vincy considerable good.

It certainly affected him strongly as he walked toward Lowick. His light, hopeful nature had perhaps never been so bruised as by the suggestion that, without him in the way, Mary could have made an excellent marriage. He was also vexed at having been, as he called it, such a stupid fool as to ask Mr. Farebrother to intervene. But no lover could have kept this new worry about Mary’s feelings from overtaking every other concern; Fred certainly could not. Despite his trust in Mr. Farebrother’s generosity, and despite what Mary had said through him, Fred could not shake the feeling that he had a rival. This was a new awareness, and he disliked it intensely. He had no readiness at all to give Mary up for her own good. He was quite ready, instead, to fight any man for her. Fighting Mr. Farebrother, however, would have to be metaphorical, which was much harder for Fred than a contest of muscles. The experience disciplined him almost as sharply as the disappointment of his uncle’s will. The iron had not entered his soul, but he had begun to imagine its cutting edge. It never occurred to him that Mrs. Garth might be mistaken about Mr. Farebrother. He did suspect she might be mistaken about Mary. Since Mary had lately been staying at the parsonage, her mother might know very little of what had been going through her mind.

Finding Mary cheerful in the drawing room with the three ladies did not reassure him. They had been talking animatedly about something they dropped as he entered. Mary was copying labels from a pile of shallow cabinet drawers in the tiny handwriting at which she excelled. Mr. Farebrother was somewhere in the village, and the three ladies knew nothing of Fred’s special relationship with Mary. Neither of them could suggest a walk in the garden. Fred predicted that he would have to leave without a private word. He first told her Christy was home, then that he had arranged to work for her father. It comforted him to see how deeply the latter news moved her. “I’m so glad,” she said quickly, then bent over her writing to hide her face. But Mrs. Farebrother could not let such a subject pass.

“Surely, my dear Miss Garth, you don’t mean you’re glad a young man is abandoning the Church for which he was educated. You only mean that, since this is how matters stand, you’re glad he’ll be working under an excellent man like your father.”

“No, Mrs. Farebrother, I’m afraid I really am glad about both,” said Mary, skillfully disposing of one disobedient tear. “My mind is dreadfully secular. I’ve never liked a clergyman except the Vicar of Wakefield and Mr. Farebrother.”

“But why, my dear?” Mrs. Farebrother stopped her large wooden knitting needles and looked at Mary. “You always have good reasons for your opinions, but this amazes me. Naturally, I exclude those who preach new doctrines. But why should you dislike clergymen?”
“Oh dear,” Mary said, appearing to think for a moment before her face broke into amusement. “I don’t like their neckcloths.”
“Then you don’t like Camden’s?” Miss Winifred asked anxiously.
“Yes, I do,” said Mary. “It’s the other clergymen’s neckcloths I dislike, because they’re the ones wearing them.”
“How very confusing!” said Miss Noble, suspecting that her own intelligence was at fault.
“My dear, you’re joking. You would need better reasons to dismiss such a respectable group of men,” Mrs. Farebrother declared majestically.
“Miss Garth has such strict ideas of what people ought to be that it’s hard to satisfy her,” Fred said.
“Well, at least I’m pleased she makes an exception for my son,” the old lady replied.

Mary was wondering why Fred sounded so irritated when Mr. Farebrother entered and had to be told about Fred’s arrangement with Mr. Garth. At the end he said with quiet satisfaction, “_That’s_ right.” Then he bent over Mary’s labels and praised her handwriting. Fred felt horribly jealous. Of course he was glad Mr. Farebrother was so admirable, but he wished the man were ugly and fat, as forty-year-old men sometimes are. The outcome was obvious: Mary openly ranked Farebrother above everyone, and these women were plainly encouraging the match. Fred was certain he would have no chance to speak to Mary when Mr. Farebrother said:
“Fred, help me take these drawers back to my study. You haven’t seen my fine new study yet. Please come as well, Miss Garth. I want to show you a magnificent spider I found this morning.”

Mary immediately understood the Vicar’s purpose. Since that memorable evening, he had never departed from his old pastoral kindness toward her, and her brief wonder and uncertainty had fallen completely asleep. Mary habitually judged probabilities with some rigor. If an idea flattered her vanity, she took that as a warning to reject it as absurd, a practice in which she had gained plenty of experience early in life. Things happened as she expected. After inviting Fred to admire the study’s furnishings and Mary to admire the spider, Mr. Farebrother said:
“Stay here a moment. I’m going to find an engraving. Fred is tall enough to hang it for me. I’ll be back in a few minutes.” He left. Yet the very first thing Fred said to Mary was:
“Whatever I do, it’s useless, Mary. You’re bound to marry Farebrother in the end.” There was anger in his voice.
“What do you mean, Fred?” Mary cried indignantly. She blushed deeply, startled out of her usual quickness in answering.
“You must see it perfectly clearly—you, who see everything.”
“All I see is how badly you’re behaving, Fred, to speak like that about Mr. Farebrother when he’s done everything to plead your case. How did you get such an idea?”
Despite his irritation, Fred showed some cunning. If Mary really had suspected nothing, there was no advantage in repeating what Mrs. Garth had said.
“It’s the obvious conclusion,” he answered. “You’re constantly with a man who’s better than me at everything, and whom you put above everyone else. What fair chance can I have?”
“You’re very ungrateful, Fred,” Mary said. “I wish I’d never told Mr. Farebrother that I cared for you at all.”

“I’m not ungrateful. Without this I’d be the happiest man alive. I told your father everything, and he was wonderfully kind. He treated me like his own son. I’d work with all my heart—writing and everything—if it weren’t for this.”
“For this? What is ‘this’?” Mary asked, now imagining that something definite must have happened or been said.
“This awful certainty that Farebrother will bowl me out.” Mary’s urge to laugh softened her anger.

“Fred,” she said, peering round to catch his eyes, which he had turned sulkily away, “you’re delightfully absurd. If you weren’t such a charming simpleton, I’d be terribly tempted to play the wicked flirt and let you think someone besides you had declared his love for me.”
“Do you truly like me best, Mary?” Fred turned his affectionate gaze toward her and tried to take her hand.

“At this moment I don’t like you at all,” Mary said, stepping back and putting her hands behind her. “I only said no one alive except you has ever declared his love to me. That hardly proves any very wise man ever will,” she finished merrily.
“I wish you’d tell me you could never possibly think of him that way,” Fred said.

“Don’t ever dare bring this up with me again, Fred,” Mary said, becoming serious. “I can’t decide whether you’re more foolish or ungenerous for failing to see that Mr. Farebrother deliberately left us alone so we could talk freely. I’m disappointed that you’re so blind to his consideration.”

Before they could say more, Mr. Farebrother returned with the engraving. Fred went back to the drawing room still carrying jealous fears, but able to draw comfort from Mary’s words and manner. On the whole, their conversation hurt Mary more. Inevitably, her attention had shifted, and she could see that things might be interpreted differently. She now felt as though she were slighting Mr. Farebrother. When the man concerned is greatly respected, that feeling always threatens a grateful woman’s firmness. Having a reason to go home the next day was a relief, because Mary sincerely wanted never to doubt that she loved Fred best. When tender affection has accumulated within us over many years, the thought of exchanging it for anything else seems to diminish the worth of our lives. And we can guard our affections and our faithfulness just as we guard other treasures.

“Fred has lost every other expectation. He must keep this one,” Mary told herself, a smile curling her lips. She could not prevent passing visions of a different life: new dignity and the recognition of her worth whose absence she had often felt. But if Fred had no place in that life—if he were abandoned, looking sad because he had lost her—none of it could tempt her considered thoughts.
